hero.kicker: Open source, real time generative images
hero.sub: potocolom turns your canvas into finished images while you sketch. Run it on your own GPU for free, or let the cloud carry the weight.
features.title: Built for both worlds
features.sub: One codebase behind everything: the free install on your desk and the managed cloud are the same application.
features.f1_title: A live loop, not a queue
features.f1_body: Canvas frames go up, generated frames come down, over one WebSocket. Drawing feels like drawing.
features.f2_body: Self-host with docker compose on any NVIDIA or AMD card, or subscribe and draw on a rented fleet.
features.f3_body: Drop a model manifest and the interface adapts to its parameters. No frontend release required.
features.f4_body: No public gallery. Your images live behind signed links you can share and revoke, and your data exports in one click.
caps.title: One canvas, four jobs
caps.sub: Generation, upscaling, editing and the live loop run through the same job path, the same models and the same history, self-hosted or in the cloud.
caps.gen_body: Text to image. Pick a model and the controls come from its manifest, so a new model needs no frontend release.
caps.up_body: Take a finished image up in size with Real-ESRGAN class weights. Fast tier by default, quality tier when it matters.
caps.edit_body: Image to image: feed a picture back in with a prompt and a strength, and keep the parts that already work.
caps.live_body: Strokes go up and frames come down over one WebSocket.
gallery.sub: Sketches become finished images in real time. A sample of work from the community - the kind of output the canvas produces.
gallery.prompts_hint: Hover to pause. Click any prompt to copy it.
split.title: Free where it should be, paid where it must be
split.cloud_p1: No GPU needed, drawing in seconds
split.cloud_p3: The same application, operated for you
fork.title: Take the repo. Run it on your GPU.
fork.cmd2: cd potocolom && make setup && make deps
fork.out2: Virtualenvs built. PostgreSQL, Redis and MinIO listening.
fork.b1: The realtime drawing loop is in the repo: strokes up, renders down, on your hardware.
fork.b2: New models arrive as manifests. The interface reads their schema - no waiting on a release.
fork.b3: One compose file on NVIDIA or AMD. No account required, no public gallery, no phone-home.
footer.tagline: One AGPL codebase, self-hosted or in the cloud.
pricing.title: Simple tiers, honest credits
pricing.sub: Credits meter GPU seconds transparently: drawing drains them live, generations cost a handful each. Beta pricing, subject to change before public launch - the waitlist hears first.
pricing.t1_b3: Or a few thousand quick generations
pricing.trial: Every beta invite includes a one-time trial grant - no card needed to try.
ill.title: One sheet, two pictures
ill.sub: Print a prime image. Turn the sheet 180 degrees. A second subject appears. This is research on the same worker stack as the studio. It is not a product feature yet.
ill.hero_hint: Use Flip to turn the sheet 180 degrees.
ill.s1_p1: A flip illusion is one printable picture. Upright, it shows subject A. Turn the sheet 180 degrees. It shows subject B. The prime is the file for the printer. The two views on this page show that same sheet before and after the turn.
ill.s1_p2: The method is Diffusion Illusions (Burgert et al.). A frozen image model scores how each view matches its prompt. Only one small network trains. It paints the prime. The large model stays frozen.
ill.s1_p3: This page is the public study of that method on our worker stack. A typeset paper can follow. You can read this version now.
ill.s2_p1: The optimizer has four parts. A prime network paints each printable image. Fixed arrangements turn primes into derived views. A frozen diffusion model scores those views. Only the prime network trains. In code, the parts have these names: FourierFeatureNetwork, the ILLUSIONS flip arrangement, and DiffusionAdapter. The paper calls them prime images, arrangement processes, and the frozen model.
ill.s2_p2: Flip uses one prime and a 180-degree turn. Rotate and hidden types stack transparencies. This page shows flip only. We measured the flip type.
ill.s2_p3: Gradients never flow through the UNet. The large model stays frozen. First comes Score Distillation. Then comes Dream Target.
ill.fig_arch_cap: One prime, two arrangements, two views. Frozen SD 1.5 scores the views. Only the prime weights move.
ill.fig_families_cap: Where this method sits. Sampling-time methods combine noise estimates inside one diffusion pass. This page optimises a prime network instead, which costs far more and accepts arrangements that are not pixel permutations. The gallery at the foot is Figure 1 of Illusion3D (Feng et al., arXiv 2412.09625), cropped, used under CC BY 4.0.
ill.fig_workflow_cap: How we bake one cell. Make primes. Make flip views. Run Score Distillation. Reset Adam. Run Dream Target. Out come the prime and both views.
ill.s3_title: The prime is a small network
ill.s3_p1: Each prime is a Fourier Feature Network. Pixel coordinates go through a fixed random projection, then sine and cosine, then a small network, then sigmoid RGB. The default network uses 256 Fourier features at scale 10. Its MLP is 512-256-256-256-3, which is 263,683 weights, and it renders at 512 px. Every image on this page came from the research network instead. That one uses 128 features, four 1x1 convolutions with BatchNorm, 199,683 weights, and it renders at 256 px. Only these weights move.
ill.s3_p2: The paper shows why this matters. Pixel optimization hides the signal in high frequencies. A printer cannot hold that noise. Network-weight optimization keeps the signal in printable structure.
ill.fig_ffn_cap: Pixel coordinates go in. Printable RGB comes out. The chain shows the network that painted this gallery. The CLI default differs, and the figure says how.
ill.s4_p1: Phase 1 uses frozen Stable Diffusion 1.5. The step encodes each derived view to latents. It adds noise at a random timestep. The frozen UNet scores the noised latents with high classifier-free guidance. One doubled UNet forward covers all views, unless the view batch size splits it into chunks. The default guidance is 100. This gallery ran 60. Timesteps are integers between 2 percent and 98 percent of the schedule.
ill.s4_p2: The step applies the guided noise residual as a gradient on those latents. That gradient updates only the prime network. The paper printed pseudocode has no gradient path. The authors' code uses residual-as-gradient. Every SDS implementation uses that form.
ill.fig_sds_cap: One distillation step. Encode the view. Add noise. Run the frozen UNet one time. The residual becomes the gradient. It reaches the prime weights only.
ill.fig_symbols_cap: Every symbol the figures use, with the value or shape it carries and the function that computes it.
ill.s5_p1: Phase 2 is Dream Target. It uses DreamShaper LCM. Each round asks img2img for a cleaner target. Then SSIM and MSE pull the derived views toward that target. Strength starts high and decays to a light polish.
ill.s5_p2: The optimizer CLI defaults are {codeSds} SDS steps and {codeDream} Dream rounds. We baked the gallery with a research recipe. It uses {researchSds} SDS steps and {researchDream} Dream round. That recipe is not only a step budget. It also swaps the prime network, the phase 1 optimizer, the guidance, and the SDS objective. Read every number on a figure with that in mind.
ill.s5_p3: The loop creates a fresh Adam optimizer at the phase boundary. SDS gradients are about four orders of magnitude larger than Dream Target gradients. Without the reset, phase 2 moved loss by under {adamWithout} percent per round. With the reset, loss moved {adamLow} to {adamHigh} percent. Those figures come from a short flip run. The run used {adamSds} SDS steps and {adamDream} Dream Target rounds of {adamDreamSteps} steps each.
ill.fig_loop_cap: Real checkpoints from the calibration smoke run. SDS 250 shows noise. SDS 5000 shows a giraffe. The loss swings sign the whole time, so it cannot rank quality.
ill.fig_dream_cap: A real round-1 triple. It shows the derived view, the dreamed target, and the regressed view.
ill.s6_p1: Independent Dream Targets can fight over the same pixels. Joint Dream denoises both flip views together. It averages them in the upright frame. Then it steps from that consensus. The two views become two orientations of one image. Pixel space is required for this step because the SD 1.5 VAE does not commute with a 180-degree turn.
ill.s6_p2: The loop averages in pixel space. The SD 1.5 VAE does not commute with a 180-degree turn in latent space. Joint Dream is an opt-in flag. It is not the product default. It can rescue a pair whose shapes can be one picture. It can also collapse a pair whose subjects cannot share one picture.
ill.fig_joint_cap: Both views denoise together and reconcile to one consensus image in pixel space. Independent targets disagree. Joint targets are one image seen two ways.
ill.s7_p1: A good result is a specific pair, seed, and viewing mode. It is not a recipe that works every time. We pick keepers by eye. An automatic CLIP screen failed. Its ROC-AUC was {auc} against a {bar} bar. So we do not use it.
ill.s7_p2: Prompt wording is the biggest lever. Arguments do not predict it. Frames and extra objects come from the specific phrase. They do not come from sketch versus oil as a medium. We kept oil for color and for fewer photographic frames. We did not keep oil because it won on yield.
ill.s7_p3: We rejected negative prompts. Extra Dream rounds after the first made images worse. 256 px primes were enough. 512 px cost about {cost} times as much for no visible gain. That is the prime render resolution, not the Score Distillation ladder.
ill.s7_p4: These conclusions came after the gallery was baked. The {galleryCount} keepers in the gallery span both wordings and both styles. {jointCount} of {galleryCount} used joint Dream. The rest used independent targets. Export {export}.
ill.fig_review_cap: 206 cells, 43 at score four or five, 26 keepers. A frame defect cut 16 of them, and one was never frame-rated. CLIP scores are recorded. They are not a gate.
ill.fig_seeds_cap: One pair at three seeds, baked twice. Joint Dream on top, independent targets below. Nothing else changes, and the human score runs from zero to five.
ill.fig_failures_cap: Three real cells that did not become keepers, each with both views and the reason it was cut.
ill.fig_recipe_cap: The shipped defaults against the recipe that baked this gallery. The recipe changes the network, the optimizer, the guidance, and the objective.
ill.s8_p1: {showcaseCount} illusions, each scored {minScore} or {score} in a blind review. {galleryCount} are keepers from export {export}. The rest scored as well but come from other exports and middle stages, and most have no frame rating yet. Click an image, or Flip, to turn the sheet. A good seed does not promise that the same pair will work on a new one.
ill.s9_p1: For flip, print the prime on paper. Turn the sheet around. Laser output is enough for a desk test. Rotate and hidden types need transparency film and a backlight. They are not on this page.
ill.fig_print_cap: Print the prime. Then turn the sheet 180 degrees.
ill.s10_p1: There is no illusion job in the API. There is no designer in the app. The optimizer is a worker CLI on an unmerged branch. This page is the public study of that research.
ill.s10_p2: When jobs land, they will sit behind realtime drawing sessions. Other batch work sits there too. Until then, the live product is still the canvas loop in the whitepaper.
ill.s10_p3: A typeset paper can follow. This page is the public study until then.
ill.attr: Images generated with Stable Diffusion 1.5 and DreamShaper LCM (CreativeML Open RAIL-M).
bench.title: Model runtime on {vram} GB VRAM
bench.sub: Curated prompts, fixed parameter variants, one model loaded at a time. GPU milliseconds are measured on the worker; wall time includes queue and I/O.
bench.empty_body: Run make benchmark on a GPU worker, then make benchmark-publish to copy results.json into the site.
bench.summary_note: Load time is paid once per model. GPU time is denoising only. Wall time is end-to-end per image.
bench.by_prompt_note: Average GPU time across variants for each curated prompt.
bench.specs_note: Hardware and license requirements from worker manifests. VRAM is for full GPU residency; lower-VRAM cards may use CPU offload at reduced speed.
bench.charts_note: Ranked by GPU denoise time. The median sits beside the average so a skewed run shows up; expand a model below for the per-prompt breakdown.
bench.leaderboard_note: Models ranked fastest to slowest by average GPU denoise time on this hardware.
bench.chart_grouped_desc: One axis per model, ranked fastest first. The inner ring is GPU denoise time, the outer one is end-to-end wall time, so the gap between them is the overhead around denoising.
bench.chart_spread_desc: One dot per prompt category on each model row, placed by average GPU denoise time. How far the dots scatter is the variation the averages above hide.
bench.details_note: Expand a model for variant and prompt tables.
wp.title: How potocolom works
wp.sub: What happens between a stroke on the canvas and the pixels coming back: the platform's anatomy, the realtime loop, GPU scheduling, the model system, and the safety, privacy and billing machinery. Everything on this page is specified in the public docs and recorded as decisions.
wp.s1_title: A live brush, not a prompt queue
wp.s1_p1: potocolom turns an image model into a drawing partner. You sketch on a canvas and a diffusion model re-renders your strokes as a finished image while you draw, several times per second, not once after a button press. The prompt sets the scene; your strokes decide the composition.
wp.s1_p2: Around that loop sits a full studio: classic prompt-to-image generation with per-model controls, one-click upscaling, a history of everything you make, laid out as a canvas of how each image was derived, and a star for the keepers. This page explains the machinery underneath, in the order a stroke meets it.
wp.s2_p1: Three moving parts. The studio runs in your browser. The platform API is a stateless relay and scheduler: it owns no GPU; it routes realtime frames, dispatches work and keeps the authoritative record of every job and asset in PostgreSQL. GPU workers hold the models and do the actual rendering.
wp.s2_p2: Workers always dial out to the platform over one persistent WebSocket. Because the connection starts on the worker's side, a GPU machine needs no inbound ports, no public address and no firewall exceptions. Any machine that can open a connection can serve, from a data-center card to the desktop under your desk.
wp.s2_p3: On connect, a worker announces its models in a manifest: capabilities, parameter schema, VRAM needs. The platform validates every request against that schema, picks a worker that serves the model, and streams progress back live. Finished images stay off the realtime channel: workers upload them to a one-time upload target, and your browser loads them through a link that expires in minutes when storage is S3, or through the API's owner-checked file route on a local disk. With S3 storage the API reads each finished image once to verify it, but never serves the bytes itself. If the platform restarts, it rebuilds its queue from the database and carries on.
wp.s1_p3: The map below follows one stroke through the system. Your canvas sends a frame to the platform, the platform hands it to a GPU slot running a model described by its manifest, and the generated frame comes back the same way. Finished images take a separate road through storage. Each stop carries the number of the section that explains it: the anatomy of the platform, the realtime loop, GPU scheduling, models, images and privacy, credits, and what happens when something fails.
wp.s1_p4: Not every part is running yet. The self-hosted platform works today on your own GPU. Parts of the hosted cloud, such as the admission queue, idle release, the billing service and relaying across several API servers, are designed and specified but not yet built. Where a section describes one of those, it says so.
wp.s2_p4: Two WebSockets carry everything live. The browser's carries canvas frames up and generated frames down as binary WebP, each behind a small header: a one-byte type and the 16-byte session id. The platform checks that every frame belongs to the session it names before relaying it, because the browser is untrusted. The worker's socket opens with its hello and manifest, then carries session control, canvas and generated frames, jobs and progress in both directions.
wp.s2_p5: PostgreSQL holds the record of every job and asset, and nothing else is trusted to. After a restart, a job that was running is retried once or marked failed, and queued jobs are pushed back from the database. A worker that falls silent for 90 seconds is closed: its jobs go back to the queue, and its drawing sessions move to another worker with room.
wp.s3_p4: Opening a session is one decision. The platform checks your prompt and parameters against the model's schema, then looks for room on a worker that holds a realtime model fully in memory. If there is one, the worker readies the session, the platform waits at most ten seconds for its answer, and the loop starts. If no worker has room, the session is refused today. The hosted service is designed to queue it instead, with a live position, and to treat that queue as the signal to bring another GPU online.
wp.s3_p5: A session is live while you draw. If its worker disappears it is interrupted, then resumed on another worker with room, and the studio re-sends the whole current canvas, so nothing is lost; with no other worker, as on a one-GPU install, the session ends today. The design adds two states: queued, while a session waits for a slot, and idle, once its slot is released. In the hosted service, credits are designed to meter only while a session is active, reserved about 60 GPU-seconds at a time, so waiting and idle time cost nothing.
wp.s4_p4: The specified scheduler is one loop, run by a single leader among the API replicas, in a fixed order. First it reconciles: a worker whose heartbeat has lapsed is forgotten, its jobs requeue once and its sessions move to another machine. Then it releases sessions idle for 60 seconds, so metering stops. Then it admits waiting sessions into free slots. Last, it fills the remaining capacity with queued jobs. Today one in-process loop dispatches queued jobs; the leader lease, admission queue and idle release are still designed.
wp.s4_p5: Inside one worker, memory management is real today. The worker reads free VRAM live and keeps several models warm; before loading another it evicts the least recently used one rather than push the new model onto a slower offload rung. Warm models still take turns on one GPU lock, so keeping them resident saves switching time, not compute. Only a fully resident model may serve drawing sessions, and at warmup the worker times its frames and advertises the most sessions whose p95 frame time still meets the 2 fps floor.
wp.s5_p4: The manifest is split by who needs it. The recipe (weight source, VAE, scheduler and LoRA) is read only by the worker, which builds the pipeline from it and strips it before announcing the manifest, so weight locations never cross the wire. The platform receives the rest: identity, capabilities as the routing key, the VRAM requirement, license fields and the parameter schema. The API checks every request against that schema and rejects an invalid one before any GPU time is spent; the studio reads the ranges, defaults and size options of its fixed controls from the same schema.
wp.s5_p5: The VRAM figure in a manifest is the model's own need for full residency, not a promise about any card. The worker compares it with the memory it actually has free and picks a rung: fully resident, offloaded to system memory in whole components, or streamed layer by layer from system memory or disk. Offloading lets a small card run a large model slowly, but it drops the model from drawing, because only full residency holds the frame bar.
wp.s6_p5: Follow one generation through the figure. The prompt and your canvas go to a GPU worker, and while you draw, frames come back as WebP. The finished result is written once as a lossless PNG master with a WebP thumbnail, next to a record of its parameters (with the seed, when you set one) and parent image, under a storage key built from your account and an unguessable job id. It reaches your browser only through the delivery route above, and anyone else only if you create a share link.
wp.s7_p4: Every charge is specified to follow one contract: a reservation with three possible endings. The API picks the reservation id and sends it with an estimate and a time limit, so a call that times out can be retried with the same id without booking twice. The reservation then ends exactly once: committed with the actual GPU time, refunded when the work fails, or expired when the time limit passes with neither, which returns credits a crash would otherwise strand. Repeating a step does nothing; a conflicting step is refused.
wp.s7_p5: A drawing session is designed to use the same contract in chunks. About 60 GPU-seconds are reserved at admission and extended chunk by chunk while you draw, and the actual use is committed when the session goes idle or closes. If an extension fails, the session ends gracefully with an out-of-credits message, so the most a session can overdraw is one chunk.
wp.s7_p6: When billing cannot be reached, the priorities are fixed: never hand out free GPU time, then never lose a charge. Reserving fails with a billing-unavailable error. Commits and refunds wait in an outbox table in the platform's own database and retry until billing acknowledges them, and the ledger's unique keys make a repeated delivery harmless. In the open code this contract is specified but not wired yet: there is no quota client or QUOTA_SERVICE_URL setting today, and GPU time is recorded for analytics only.
wp.s8_p3: Compute failures, a worker lost mid-job or mid-session, are handled in the open code today: the lost job is requeued exactly once, and a second failure leaves the job marked failed in your history. The retry button and the refund that goes with it are designed for the hosted service. Money failures, a renewal that fails or a billing service that cannot be reached, are designed never to claw back credit already granted and never to grant GPU time on credit. Infrastructure failures hit a limit, not a bill.
wp.s8_p4: Those limits are recorded decisions for the hosted service, not yet running. The fleet autoscaler has a hard machine ceiling and a monthly budget, so demand past them waits in the admission queue behind a high-demand banner instead of renting more. The database runs in one availability zone with point-in-time recovery, accepting up to five minutes of lost writes and about an hour of manual recovery if that zone fails. The money rows depend on the billing service, which is also designed and not built yet.
wp.s9_p3: Running it yourself is the same software, not a lite edition. A release is designed to produce one set of container images and one static studio build, which self-hosters would pull from GHCR and the cloud would mirror by digest; publishing is not wired yet, so today you build the images from the repository. Application code never asks which deployment it is in. It reads specific settings, and the studio adapts to what GET /api/v1/config returns.
wp.s9_p4: Where the two deployments must differ, a seam owns the difference, with a self-hosted and a cloud implementation. Storage is the local disk or S3, and auth is none or accounts; both switch with one setting today. Job queues live inside one process, frames pass between sockets in one API process, and there is no quota check. Their cloud versions, Redis queues, a Redis pub/sub relay between API replicas and a billing service, are designed and not built yet.
wp.s9_p5: Billing, the GPU fleet autoscaler and the cloud infrastructure code belong to a separate private repository, and the billing service there is not built yet. That code must never import a line of the open code: it is written against a documented HTTP contract, versioned under /v1 like the worker protocol. The boundary is a process boundary, so the open code stays AGPL and complete on its own, and anyone can read the contract the private side must honor.
wp.fig_arch_cap: The three moving parts. Frames flow through the relay; finished images go straight between workers, storage and your browser with S3 storage, and through the API on a local install.
wp.s3_p1: While you draw, the canvas is snapshotted and sent as a compact binary frame (a small header plus WebP pixels) on the same WebSocket that brings results back. A distilled diffusion model re-renders it in a handful of denoising steps at 512 px, and generated frames stream back at 2 to 4 per second.
wp.s3_p2: The loop never queues stale input: if a new stroke arrives while the GPU is busy, it replaces the pending frame rather than lining up behind it. Latest input wins; superseded frames are simply dropped. You always see the newest state of your drawing, never a replay of where it was.
wp.s3_p3: Sessions are admitted only while a worker's measured frame budget has room, and are never oversubscribed. If the machine under your session vanishes and another has room, the platform reassigns you, the canvas is re-sent, and drawing continues. Idle release is designed but not running yet: after about a minute without a stroke your slot would be freed, the canvas would stay in the browser, and the next stroke would reacquire one.
wp.fig_loop_cap: Admission, the frame loop and worker-loss recovery as they run today; dashed parts, the admission queue, idle release and credit metering, are designed but not built yet.
wp.s4_p1: GPU seconds are the scarce resource, so scheduling is specified rather than improvised. Realtime sessions come first and are never oversubscribed: the platform gives a worker a new session only while its measured frame times still fit the 2 fps bar, and a full pool turns a new session away. In the specified design, queued generations fill whatever capacity is idle and pause between denoising steps when a drawing session needs the slot; nothing ever preempts an active session. That preemption is designed, not built yet: today jobs and sessions simply share the worker.
wp.s4_p2: How many sessions one GPU can hold is measured, not guessed: at warmup a worker benchmarks its models and advertises the concurrency it can sustain while keeping frame pacing above the bar.
wp.s4_p3: Model placement is designed to follow demand. A hot set of fast models would stay pinned in VRAM for instant sessions, and everything else would load on demand, with a visible loading state of about a minute the first time. When the pool is genuinely full, new sessions would wait in an admission queue with a live position, and that queue would be the signal that brings more GPUs online. This fleet-level placement is not built yet; what runs today is the memory management inside each worker, described below.
wp.s5_p1: A model, to the platform, is a JSON manifest: what it can do, how much VRAM it needs, and a parameters block that is standard JSON Schema. That schema is the single source of truth: the platform validates every request against it and the studio sizes its controls from it, so a model that uses the standard parameters becomes usable everywhere, with the right ranges, without touching a line of frontend code.
wp.s5_p2: Manifests also carry the recipe: distilled few-step models (the Turbo and LCM class) for the drawing loop, Lightning-distilled models for fast queued stills, heavier samplers for quality renders, optional scheduler overrides and fused acceleration LoRAs. On a single consumer 16 GB card, once warm, the fast class renders a 512 px image in under three tenths of a second, the Lightning class takes a few seconds at 1024 px, and the default quality model, SDXL, about twelve seconds. The numbers are not marketing: they come from a benchmark harness anyone can run, and the results are published on the live benchmark page.
wp.s5_p3: Models ship only after their licenses are vetted. Each manifest can record its license, its attribution text and a commercial revenue cap, and the studio shows a required attribution next to the model.
wp.s6_p1: Transport and storage have different jobs, so they use different formats: canvas and generated frames travel as WebP, chosen for quality per byte at interactive speeds, while the stored master of every generation is lossless PNG, the archival copy of your work, with WebP thumbnails for fast browsing. Every generation stores its parameters next to the image, including the seed when you set one, so a seeded result can be reproduced, and provenance is recorded in the schema so an image can tell where it came from.
wp.s6_p2: Assets are private by default; sharing is an explicit act. In the cloud they are delivered through signed URLs that expire after five minutes, and a self-hosted install serves them through the API's own file route. Signed-in state is an opaque server-side token in an HttpOnly cookie, invisible to page scripts, listable and instantly revocable. Nothing you create is used to train models.
wp.s6_p3: Content safety for the hosted service is designed, not built yet. The design screens every prompt through layers (normalization, then rules, then a classifier) on every path a prompt can take, including live drawing, and enforces on strikes without retaining prompt text. No screening code runs today, in either deployment.
wp.s6_p4: The platform measures itself without watching you: no tracking cookies (the cookies it sets serve sign-in and remember the studio sidebar), no trackers, not a line of client-side analytics. Usage statistics are rows the server already knows (which model ran, for how long, and a category label meant to come from a CLIP pass over the output image), never the prompt, the image, or your address. The label field is wired, but the CLIP pass is not built yet, so every row reads other today. Self-hosted installs send one anonymous daily aggregate that can be previewed locally and disabled with a single switch.
wp.s7_p1: The hosted service is designed to meter usage in credits, and none of this runs yet. A credit corresponds to GPU time actually spent. Before any GPU second is spent, the platform would reserve an estimate; when the work finishes, it would commit the actual amount, and failed work would refund automatically. Drawing sessions would meter in small chunks only while active, so an idle canvas costs nothing.
wp.s7_p2: Every money path is designed to tolerate replay. Payment webhooks deduplicate on event ids, the credit ledger is append-only with unique source keys, and reservations are idempotent with a timeout that returns stranded credits on its own. Retries and redeliveries are no-ops by construction.
wp.s7_p3: Payment pages are to be hosted by the payment provider, so card data never touches platform servers. If billing is ever unreachable, reserving is designed to fail closed, so no GPU time is granted on credit, while finished work settles through a retry queue until it lands exactly once.
wp.fig_credits_cap: The hosted billing design: money in, the append-only ledger, and money out through the quota contract. None of it is wired in the open-source build yet.
wp.s8_p1: GPU machines vanish; the design treats that as normal. A worker dying mid-generation gets the job requeued exactly once before it fails visibly, so an input that crashes workers cannot burn GPU time in a loop. A worker dying mid-session triggers a transparent resume when another machine has room: it takes over and your canvas is re-sent.
wp.s8_p2: The platform restarting rebuilds its queue from the database. The database being down degrades the service instead of stopping it: drawing sessions already open keep running, and on an install without accounts new ones still open, while history waits. Retries are bounded, and the hosted service is designed so failed work refunds and no failure mode produces a surprise bill.
wp.fig_failures_cap: Every failure, what you see, and what the money does. Compute recovery runs today; the money and infrastructure rows are recorded designs for the hosted service.
wp.fig_journey_cap: One stroke, end to end. Each number marks the section below that explains that stop.
wp.fig_gpu_cap: One GPU, two kinds of work: drawing sessions hold measured slots on fully resident models and queued jobs share the rest; pausing jobs for a session, the scheduler loop and scaling out are designed, shown dashed.
wp.fig_manifest_cap: One JSON file per model: the worker builds the pipeline from its recipe, the platform routes requests by model and capability and validates them with its schema, and the studio sizes its controls from the same schema.
wp.fig_images_cap: What happens to a prompt and an image: WebP frames in transit, and a private lossless PNG with its parameters, delivered by a short-lived signed URL in the cloud or the API's own route on a local install. Prompt screening is designed, not built yet.
wp.fig_deploy_cap: One codebase, two deployments: every difference is designed to be one setting behind a seam, and the private billing and fleet services are to be reached only over HTTP.
wp.s9_p1: The product is AGPL 3.0 and complete on its own: the code that serves you, including this page, is the code in the repository, and you can run the entire platform on your own GPU.
wp.s9_p2: The design is public too: the architecture documents, the wire protocol, the benchmark methodology, and a decision ledger that records not only every choice but the alternatives that were rejected and why.
wp.cta_docs: Read the full docs on GitHub

faq.title: A few things to know
faq.sub: The short version of how the studio, the hardware and the hosted service fit together.
faq.a1: An open source image studio built around a live drawing loop. You sketch and write a prompt; a diffusion model continuously re-renders the canvas. The same studio also handles generation, editing and upscaling.
faq.a2: No. The AGPL 3.0 repository contains the complete application. Run it with Docker Compose on a supported NVIDIA or AMD GPU, without an account or required phone-home. The paid cloud is the same product operated for you.
faq.q3: Which models and GPUs can I use?
faq.a3: Models arrive through manifests that declare their controls, licenses and VRAM needs. The current Studio catalogue includes SDXL-based Stability AI models, realtime and fast variants, and Real-ESRGAN upscalers on NVIDIA or AMD hardware. The benchmark page publishes measured requirements and speeds.
faq.a4: Assets are private by default and served through short-lived signed links. Sharing is explicit, your data can be exported, and your work is not used to train models.
faq.q5: How will the cloud beta and credits work?
faq.a5: The cloud meters actual GPU time. Active drawing and GPU work consume credits; an idle canvas does not, and failed work refunds automatically. Beta invitations include a trial grant with no card required.
